solution:
A is benzyl cyanide (phenylethanenitrile) and B is 2-phenylethanamine.

Alcoholic KCN replaces the bromine of benzyl bromide by a cyanide group, and the nitrile so formed is then reduced by sodium and ethanol - the Mendius reduction of section 13.3.3, \(\mathrm{R-C}\equiv\mathrm{N} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-CH_2-NH_2}\), which adds one carbon to the amine chain relative to the original halide:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Br} + \mathrm{KCN} \xrightarrow{\text{alcohol}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2-C}\equiv\mathrm{N} + \mathrm{KBr}\)

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2-C}\equiv\mathrm{N} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Na/C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\)

This is the same two-stage sequence the chapter uses in its worked example to convert methyl bromide into ethylamine.

Section 13.5 traces the basic nature of amines to the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen, and the chapter presents it in both of the usual senses.

As a LEWIS base, the amine shares that lone pair with an electron-deficient species. The chapter's example is trimethylamine and boron trifluoride:

\(\mathrm{Me_3N{:}} + \mathrm{BF_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Me_3N^{\oplus}\text{-}BF_3^{\ominus}}\)

As a LOWRY-BRONSTED base, the amine accepts a proton from water:

\(\mathrm{{\gg}N{:}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{{\gg}N^{\oplus}\text{-}H} + \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\)

For methylamine this reads \(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3-NH_3^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\); the strength of the base is measured by \(\mathrm{K_b}\), or equivalently by \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), which is 3.38 for methanamine (Table 13.4). The stronger the base, the further right this equilibrium lies, the larger \(\mathrm{K_b}\) and the smaller \(\mathrm{pK_b}\).

The basic character is also what the laboratory test of section 13.6.1(a) detects: an aqueous solution of a water-soluble amine turns red litmus blue, and a water-insoluble amine dissolves in aqueous HCl as its substituted ammonium chloride, from which excess aqueous NaOH regenerates the free amine.

Diazotisation is the conversion of an aromatic primary amine into its arene diazonium salt by treatment with nitrous acid at low temperature. Section 13.6.6 explains that nitrous acid is unstable and so is prepared in situ by adding aqueous sodium nitrite to hydrochloric acid already mixed with the amine, and section 13.6.6(b) adds that the aromatic diazonium salts so formed 'have reasonable stability at 273 K' - unlike the aliphatic ones, which decompose at once.

For aniline:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(NaNO_2 + HCl)}]{273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N}\equiv\mathrm{N^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}}\)

The product is benzene diazonium chloride. Written with all products shown, the equation balances as \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\); the chapter prints only the first form.

Acetic acid has two carbon atoms and methylamine has one, so this is a step-down conversion and the chapter's Hofmann bromamide degradation (section 13.3.6) is the reaction that achieves it. The acid is first converted to its amide, which is then degraded:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-COONH_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta,\ -\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2}\)  (acetamide)

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The second step is printed in the chapter verbatim as its worked example of Hofmann degradation, acetamide giving methylamine. [Note: the first step, carboxylic acid to amide via the ammonium salt, is not shown in this chapter; it comes from the carboxylic acid chapter.]

Section 13.7.2 describes coupling as the second class of reaction of arene diazonium salts, the one in which the diazo group is RETAINED.

When an arene diazonium salt is treated with a reactive aromatic compound such as a phenol or an aromatic amine, an azo compound is formed in which two aromatic rings are joined through the azo group \(\mathrm{-N=N-}\). The reaction is called azo coupling. It is an electrophilic aromatic substitution in which the electrophile is the positively charged diazonium ion, and substitution usually occurs para to the ring-activating group of the other ring. The extended conjugation of the product makes azo compounds brightly coloured, and they are used as dyes; the chapter notes that the acid-base indicator methyl orange is an azo dye.

The two examples printed in the chapter are:

1. With phenol, in mild alkaline medium: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-N}\equiv\mathrm{N^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}} + \mathrm{C_6H_5-OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-OH} + \mathrm{HCl}\), giving p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye.

2. With aniline, in mild alkaline medium: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-N}\equiv\mathrm{N^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}} + \mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-NH_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\), giving p-aminoazobenzene, a yellow dye.

Coupling with beta-naphthol in NaOH is used as a confirmatory test for primary aromatic amines, the orange dye test of section 13.6.1(b).

Gabriel phthalimide synthesis (section 13.3.5) is a method for preparing a PRIMARY amine, and the chapter sets it out in three stages.

Stage 1 - Formation of the potassium salt of phthalimide: phthalimide is treated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, which removes the acidic hydrogen on nitrogen and gives potassium phthalimide.

Stage 2 - Formation of N-alkylphthalimide: the potassium salt is treated with an alkyl halide \(\mathrm{R-X}\); the phthalimide anion displaces the halide and potassium halide is eliminated.

Stage 3 - Alkaline hydrolysis: the N-alkylphthalimide is hydrolysed with aqueous NaOH to give sodium phthalate together with the primary amine \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\).

Because the alkyl group is delivered by a nucleophilic substitution on the alkyl halide, only one group can be attached to nitrogen and the product is a pure primary amine, free of the secondary and tertiary amines that ammonolysis produces. The chapter also notes the method's limitation: 'Aromatic amines cannot be prepared by this method because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the anion formed by phthalimide.'

Section 13.6.5: aliphatic or aromatic PRIMARY amines, on heating with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide, give foul (offensive) smelling products called alkyl or aryl isocyanides, also called carbylamines. The general equation is

\(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Examples:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)  (methyl isocyanide, from methylamine)

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)  (phenyl isocyanide, from aniline)

The reaction consumes both hydrogen atoms of the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group, which is why it works only for primary amines. The chapter states that it is a test for primary amines and that secondary and tertiary amines do not give it; the offensive smell of the isocyanide is what makes the test easy to observe.

(i) Methanamine into ethanamine. This adds a carbon, so it is a step-up conversion and needs the cyanide route of section 13.3.3. The amine is first converted to the alcohol by nitrous acid (section 13.6.6a), the alcohol to the halide, and the halide is then taken through the nitrile:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(NaNO_2 + HCl)}]{\mathrm{HNO_2}} \mathrm{CH_3-OH} + \mathrm{N_2}\uparrow \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{CH_3-Cl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{CH_3-C}\equiv\mathrm{N} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Na/C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\)

The last two steps are exactly the chapter's own worked example converting methyl bromide into ethylamine. [Note: the alcohol-to-halide step is not shown in this chapter; it comes from the halogen derivatives chapter.]

(ii) Aniline into p-bromoaniline. Aniline itself cannot be monobrominated, because the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group is so strongly ring activating that bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (section 13.9a). The amino group is therefore first protected by acetylation, which draws its lone pair into the acetyl group and reduces the ring activation, and is regenerated afterwards by hydrolysis:

Aniline \(\xrightarrow[\text{base}]{\mathrm{CH_3-CO-Cl}}\) acetanilide \(\xrightarrow[\text{(acetic acid solvent)}]{\mathrm{Br_2}}\) p-bromoacetanilide \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}]{\text{hydrolysis}}\) p-bromoaniline

This is the scheme worked out in the chapter's own solved problem on preparation of p-bromoaniline.

a. This is the mild reduction of Table 13.5, in which ethanol acts as the reducing agent and the diazo group is displaced by hydrogen:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{N_2}\uparrow + \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The products are benzene, nitrogen, acetaldehyde and hydrogen chloride.

b. Bromination of aniline, section 13.9(a). The amino group is a powerful ring-activating, ortho- and para-directing group, so all three of those positions are substituted and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline is obtained:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 3\mathrm{Br_2(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2(NH_2)Br_3} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

The product is 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

Section 13.3.1: when an alkyl halide is heated with an alcoholic solution of excess ammonia it undergoes nucleophilic substitution in which the halogen atom is replaced by an amino \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group to form a primary amine. This breaking of the C-X bond by ammonia is called ammonolysis; it is also described as alkylation of ammonia, and it is carried out in a sealed tube at 373 K.

\(\mathrm{R-X} + \mathrm{NH_3}\ \text{(alc., excess)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NH_2}\)

The order of reactivity of the alkyl halides is \(\mathrm{R-I} > \mathrm{R-Br} > \mathrm{R-Cl}\).

The method has a built-in drawback that the chapter is careful to state: the primary amine formed in the first step is a STRONGER nucleophile than ammonia itself, so unless ammonia is used in large excess the product reacts further with more alkyl halide to give secondary and tertiary amines and finally a quaternary ammonium salt. Ammonolysis therefore yields a mixture rather than a pure primary amine, which is why the chapter offers Gabriel phthalimide synthesis for that purpose.

Ethylamine has two carbon atoms and methylamine has one, so the conversion must lose a carbon and the chapter's Hofmann bromamide degradation (section 13.3.6), which gives 'a primary amine containing one carbon less', is the step that does it. The amine is first taken to the corresponding amide:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(NaNO_2 + HCl)}]{\mathrm{HNO_2}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{N_2}\uparrow\)

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} \xrightarrow{[\mathrm{O}]} \mathrm{CH_3-COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2}\)

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The first step (aliphatic primary amine with nitrous acid giving the alcohol and nitrogen) and the last step (acetamide giving methylamine) are both printed in this chapter. [Note: the middle steps - oxidation of the alcohol to the acid and conversion of the acid to the amide - are not shown in this chapter; they come from the alcohol and carboxylic acid chapters.]
